cues.text: An Opposite Error to Nestorius

Nearly two decades after the Council of Ephesus in 431 had condemned Nestorius for dividing Christ into two separate persons, an elderly Constantinopolitan monk named Eutyches swung theological opinion toward the opposite extreme.
He taught that after the Incarnation Christ's human nature had been so completely absorbed into his divine nature that only a single, blended nature remained — a position later called Monophysitism .
A local synod at Constantinople condemned Eutyches for this teaching in 448, but he retained powerful support, above all from Dioscorus , the ambitious Patriarch of Alexandria.
A Council Convened to Vindicate Eutyches
Emperor Theodosius II , persuaded by Dioscorus and Eutyches's allies at court, summoned a new general council to meet at Ephesus in August 449, ostensibly to resolve the dispute.

But Dioscorus, granted presidency of the assembly by imperial appointment, conducted proceedings with such open intimidation that the gathering has been remembered ever since not as a legitimate council but as the "Robber Council," the Latrocinium .
The name was coined by Pope St. Leo the Great himself in outraged protest at what had occurred.
Bullied Into Silence
Contemporary accounts describe armed soldiers and monks loyal to Dioscorus intimidating the assembled bishops into signing blank or predetermined documents.
They physically prevented dissenting voices from being heard and refused outright to have Pope Leo’s carefully argued doctrinal letter read aloud to the assembly.
The letter, his celebrated Tome , set out the orthodox teaching of Christ's two complete and unconfused natures.

Under this pressure, the council exonerated Eutyches of heresy and violently deposed several of his chief opponents, including Flavian of Constantinople, who reportedly died shortly afterward from injuries sustained in the proceedings' physical chaos.
Leo's Furious Rejection
Pope Leo the Great refused categorically to recognize the council's acts, writing to the Empress Pulcheria and others in terms of open alarm.
He called the council's proceedings a triumph of violence over frank deliberation and worked immediately to convene a genuine ecumenical council.
That council could reverse its findings and vindicate the orthodox Christology his own Tome had set out.
That vindication came only two years later, at the Council of Chalcedon in 451.
It formally annulled the Robber Council's decrees, restored its deposed bishops, and condemned both Eutyches and Dioscorus.
The council defined, with lasting authority, the doctrine of Christ's two natures united without confusion in a single Person.
Legacy
The Robber Council of Ephesus stands, in the memory of the Church, as the clearest cautionary tale within the whole conciliar tradition.

It shows what happens when a council abandons candid, free deliberation for coercion and predetermined outcome—a genuine council's form and imperial summons employed to produce not a discerned consensus of the Church's bishops but a manufactured verdict imposed by force.

Its swift and total reversal at Chalcedon reassured the Church that a council's true authority rests not in the mere fact of an emperor's convocation but in the clear-eyed, uncoerced exercise of the bishops' own apostolic judgment.
